summary: Defines LoST, an XML-based protocol that maps a service identifier and a location, geodetic or civic, to service contact URIs. It can find the right Public Safety Answering Point for emergency calls. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: LoST maps a service and a place to the contact address responsible for that location. A phone can use it to find the emergency call center that serves where the caller is.

questions: how do emergency calls find the right psap
how does lost find the right psap
what is a service boundary in lost
subtitle: How a client combines a service name with its location to find the contact address responsible for that place.

tldr.problem: Some services depend on both what the caller needs and where they are. For emergency calls, the right Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP) is the one with jurisdiction over that location, not necessarily the nearest one.
tldr.mechanism: A LoST client sends an XML request with a service URN and civic or geodetic location. The server returns contact URIs, a service region and expiry information, or directs the client to another server.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5222 defines four query types and supports recursive or iterative resolution and caching. It is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 6848, RFC 8917 and RFC 9036.

facts.label: Transport
facts.value: HTTP POST over HTTP or HTTPS

today: RFC 5222 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2008 and has been updated by RFC 6848, RFC 8917 and RFC 9036. Read those updates together with this specification.

sections.title: Mapping a Place to a Service
sections.content:
Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) maps a service identifier and a civic or geodetic location to one or more service URIs. Emergency calling is a key example: the appropriate PSAP is determined by jurisdiction, which is not necessarily the closest point by road or network.

LoST messages pass between a mapping client and server over HTTP or HTTPS. The protocol defines the exchange, not how clients discover servers, how server data is replicated or how the overall service is organized.
sections.plainLanguage: The nearest emergency center may not be responsible for the caller's address. LoST uses both the requested service and the caller's location to find the responsible contact.

sections.title: Four Questions a Client Can Ask
sections.content:
<findService> requests contact URIs for a service and location. <getServiceBoundary> retrieves a boundary, <listServices> asks what services a server supports, and <listServicesByLocation> asks what services are available in a place.

Queries can be triggered when a client starts or attaches to a network, when it moves outside a cached service region, when cached data expires, or when a service is invoked. LoST supports caching and identifies the region in which a mapping remains applicable.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can ask who to contact, what area a contact serves, or which services a server knows about. It can keep an answer until its expiry time or until its location leaves the service region.

sections.title: What a Mapping Contains
sections.content:
A <mapping> describes the service region and the service URIs. It includes the service, the authoritative source and record identifiers, a last-updated time, and an expiry value. A response may also contain a display name, a service number and a boundary.

A boundary can be returned in full or by reference. A reference is a random token with at least 128 bits of entropy; if the boundary changes, the server chooses a new identifier. The response can include the request path and a <locationUsed> identifier to show which supplied location the server used.
sections.plainLanguage: A mapping is a record that says which contact applies to a service area and when the record expires. The client can receive the area itself or a reference it can use to fetch the area later.

sections.title: Finding and Validating a Service
sections.content:
A <findService> request carries a service URN and one or more locations, in preference order. The server uses the first profile it understands. With recursive resolution, the server queries other servers for the client; with iterative resolution, it can return a redirect so the client contacts the next server.

A client can request civic-address validation. The response may identify address parts as valid, invalid or unchecked. A server can also return an alternative service, a default mapping or a warning if it could only answer part of the request.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends the kind of help it needs and a place. The server may answer directly, ask another server, or report which parts of a civic address it could verify.

sections.title: Civic and Geodetic Location Profiles
sections.content:
LoST requires support for two baseline location profiles: geodetic-2d for map shapes and coordinates, and civic for a civic address. A request can include only one baseline profile, and location order indicates the client's preference.

A client using an additional profile must also include a baseline profile so a server can still understand the request. A server uses the first profile it recognizes and returns the service boundary in that same profile. A location shape can cross service areas; the RFC allows a server to return only some matching mappings rather than an unbounded number.
sections.plainLanguage: A location can be written as map coordinates or as a street address. The two baseline formats give clients and servers a shared way to exchange location information.

sections.title: Errors, Transport and Security
sections.content:
LoST uses errors when no useful answer is possible and warnings when it can provide only a partial answer. A redirect identifies another server for the client to contact. Requests use HTTP POST with the media type application/lost+xml; LoST responses, including protocol errors, are carried in HTTP 2xx responses.

TLS must be implemented and is recommended for client-server and server-server exchanges. The RFC recommends checking the server certificate identity and explains that DNS-based server discovery can still be attacked; DNSSEC or direct server-URI configuration can address that risk.
sections.plainLanguage: If a server cannot answer, it returns an error or points to another server. TLS protects the exchange, and checking the server's identity helps ensure the client is talking to the intended service.
